replacements.before: Expert Judgement as Supervision: Binary Human Labels Yield Comparable Molecular Representations under Downstream Refitting
replacements.after: Human Binary Annotations Compete with Quantitative MIC Supervision: Controlled Tests of Molecular Representation Learning for QAC Biocides

replacements.before: Binary expert annotations may offer an economical supervision signal for molecular representation learning, but their value must be assessed separately from quantitative prediction. We compared final Good/Bad expert labels with quantitative MIC supervision for quaternary ammonium compounds using a controlled partial-fine-tuning protocol. The MolFormer-XL embedding layer and four lower encoder layers remained frozen (16.0 of 44.4 M parameters), and all 532 evaluation molecules were removed from the fine-tuning sources. The resulting sources contained 740 expert-labelled molecules, 1,153 unique quantitative molecules, and 9,338 quantitative MIC records. After downstream refitting, mean Q-HERO R² was +0.269 for expert supervision and +0.312/+0.308 for molecule-level/record-level quantitative supervision; QAC-105 values remained close to zero. In direct transfer without target refitting, quantitative supervision gave stronger ranking on Q-HERO and OOD-17, while raw R² was negative. An affine recalibration fitted on the same target predictions is therefore exploratory only. The results support comparable representation quality under the evaluated downstream-refitting protocol, not equivalence of individual labels or calibrated zero-shot MIC prediction. Limitations include substantial overlap between supervision collections, unavailable individual expert votes, incomplete attribution provenance, and the small OOD-17 case study (n = 17).
replacements.after: Binary human annotations can provide useful supervision for molecular activity modelling, but useful signal, competitive prediction and causal attribution require different tests. We compare final expert Good/Bad labels with molecule-level and record-level quantitative MIC supervision, organism-matched MIC, and quantitative mammalian-cell cytotoxicity for quaternary ammonium compounds. In an archived partial-fine-tuning experiment excluding evaluation structures from all sources, downstream Q-HERO R² was 0.269 with 740 expert labels and 0.312/0.308 with 1,153 molecule-level MIC values/9,338 MIC records. New frozen-backbone interventions use identical source molecules, scaffold splits, initial weights and training budgets. On 681 common molecules, real expert labels improved external Q-HERO RMSE relative to shuffled expert labels by 0.175 log2 µM (95% scaffold-bootstrap interval −0.258 to −0.058), while continuous pooled MIC was stronger by 0.109 (0.007 to 0.210). This expert-label benefit was not reproduced on the smaller 529-molecule organism-matched panel. Direct expert scores also ranked measured potency without numerical concentrations as model targets. The evidence establishes a useful, protocol-dependent human supervision signal and practical competition under partial fine-tuning. The controlled intervention identifies an effect of supervision within the specified algorithm; it does not identify an antibacterial mechanism, a general effect of human expertise, or equivalence between individual labels and measurements.

replacements.before: A distinct and older line of work treats human expertise not as a constraint on the model but as a source of supervision in its own right. The intuition that experienced chemists possess a "gut feeling" for what constitutes a promising molecule has been formalised at least since QED, in which desirability functions were fitted to expert judgements of drug-likeness27. Such judgement is neither perfectly consistent nor bias-free, and its provenance must be recorded if annotator agreement is to be assessed. Recent work shows that human preference signals can be machine-learnable in molecular design. Here we examine a narrower, testable question: when the same chemical space is represented by binary expert labels and by quantitative MIC records, do the resulting molecular representations perform comparably after a downstream predictor is refitted? This is a controlled comparison, not a claim that a binary label is intrinsically equivalent to an individual measurement. The novelty wording in this paragraph requires a separate literature review before submission.
replacements.after: Expert knowledge can also enter a model as a supervision target. Human preference learning has already shown that chemists’ decisions can be captured and used in molecular prioritisation and design (77). The question addressed here is more specific: can coarse Good/Bad judgements compete with numerical biological measurements when learning a representation for antibacterial QAC modelling? We distinguish three propositions: the labels contain transferable activity-related information; the resulting representation is practically competitive with quantitative supervision; and changing the supervision causes a performance change under a fixed computational protocol. These propositions require separate evidence. In particular, a controlled intervention on a training procedure is distinct from identifying causal variables in molecular antibacterial action (78).

replacements.before: The bottleneck in this domain is not only the choice of architecture but also the nature of the data. Bioactivity corpora assembled from the literature are small, sparse, and protocol-heterogeneous. Values pooled across laboratories can carry substantial experimental uncertainty, which limits the accuracy of any model trained on them37-39. We therefore investigate whether a coarse categorical signal, curated by domain experts, can yield a molecular representation comparable to one learned from pooled quantitative data under a clearly specified downstream protocol. This empirical question does not assume that categorical and quantitative labels are interchangeable.
replacements.after: The bottleneck in this domain includes the definition and context of supervision. A pooled MIC value can combine different organisms, strains and assay conditions; repeated records are not independent molecules. A binary expert judgement may compress multiple observations and other considerations, but that possibility is a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated denoising mechanism. We therefore compare broad quantitative MIC, exact S. aureus MIC and 24h MTT mammalian-cell cytotoxicity as distinct numerical supervision sources. Cytotoxicity is represented by a merged CC50/IC50/EC50 field in the available ILToxDB export (79); it is a cross-endpoint comparison rather than an antibacterial measurement. No single scalar endpoint is assumed to contain the same information as an expert judgement.

replacements.before: In our previous work, we established a baseline framework for predicting QAC antibacterial activity using MolFormer-derived embeddings. Building on that framework, the present work asks how the source of supervision affects a representation. We make three bounded contributions. First, we compare binary expert and quantitative MIC supervision on closely overlapping chemical collections, distinguishing 1,153 unique molecules from 9,338 quantitative records. Second, we evaluate partially fine-tuned representations by downstream refitting on QAC-105, Q-HERO, and a small OOD-17 set, while separating representation quality from direct zero-shot ranking. Third, we provide an audit trail for data overlap, split design, and model provenance. Claims of priority or novelty beyond this controlled comparison require external literature verification before submission.
replacements.after: Building on our MolFormer-based QAC modelling framework, we test expert supervision at two levels. First, the partial-fine-tuning analysis compares final expert labels with molecule-level and record-level quantitative MIC under a shared downstream-refitting protocol. Second, new matched-molecule interventions hold the source identities, input features, initial weights, scaffold partition and training budget constant while changing supervision. Continuous MIC, binary MIC, shuffled-label and untrained-encoder controls separate label content from quantitative resolution and architecture. A further comparison of full eligible sources assesses practical performance, while explicitly retaining the effects of source size and composition. The study therefore tests the value and limits of human supervision without treating predictive attribution as a molecular causal explanation.

replacements.before: An extension of this idea that is particularly relevant to antimicrobial research is the transfer of knowledge between related biological tasks. Transfer learning and multi-task approaches, in which a model trained on one objective informs predictions on another, have proven effective in contexts ranging from protein language model fine-tuning for antimicrobial peptide classification 35 to BERT-based minimum inhibitory concentrations (MIC) regression for E. coli and S. aureus 36. In the more specific context of small-molecule antimicrobials, a stacking approach—wherein predictions from a model trained on one bacterial species are fed as features into a model for another—offers an elegant mechanism for cross-species information transfer. Such biology-informing strategies are grounded in the mechanistic insights such as non-specific membrane disruption, meaning that activity against one pathogen could encode relevant information to another. Expert annotation of these cross-domain relationships—identifying which experimental signals from one biological system carry predictive value for another—is therefore not merely a modelling convenience but a principled encoding of domain knowledge that can yield dramatic improvements in predictive accuracy.
replacements.after: Transfer across biological tasks can be informative when the relevant signals are aligned, but shared charge or a membrane-active phenotype alone does not guarantee transferability. Antimicrobial peptide fine-tuning and BERT-based MIC regression illustrate quantitative supervision strategies (35,36). Here cross-endpoint cytotoxicity supervision is evaluated empirically rather than assumed to encode antibacterial potency. Numerical performance, direct potency ranking and a causal explanation of transfer are treated as separate outcomes.

replacements.before: In this work we examined whether final binary expert annotations and quantitative MIC supervision yield comparable molecular representations for QAC activity modelling. The evidence is strongest for a controlled partial-fine-tuning matrix with evaluation molecules excluded from every fine-tuning source, and for Q-HERO as the larger external benchmark. The 17-compound OOD collection is an informative but small case study.
replacements.after: Final human Good/Bad annotations contain activity-related information that can be learned and transferred to quantitative QAC modelling. This study establishes useful signal and practical competition under a specified partial-fine-tuning protocol, then tests their limits using matched-molecule interventions and several numerical supervision definitions.

replacements.before: First, under downstream refitting, representations partially fine-tuned on 740 final expert labels achieved results comparable to those from quantitative MIC supervision on the evaluated tasks. On Q-HERO, mean R² was +0.269 for expert supervision and +0.312/+0.308 for molecule-level/record-level quantitative supervision; on QAC-105 the values were near zero. This supports an efficiency hypothesis—coarse expert supervision can preserve useful representation-level signal—but it does not establish equivalence of individual labels or a universal label-to-record exchange rate. The 9,338-record corpus represents 1,153 unique molecules and substantially overlaps the expert collection.
replacements.after: Under partial fine-tuning and downstream refitting, 740 expert-labelled molecules yield Q-HERO R² = 0.269 compared with 0.312/0.308 for 1,153 molecule-level MIC values/9,338 MIC records. This is the principal evidence that coarse human supervision can compete in representation learning. The new frozen-backbone experiment sharpens the conclusion: real expert labels outperform shuffled labels on the pooled common-molecule panel, but continuous MIC is stronger and the expert-label benefit does not reproduce on the smaller organism-matched panel. Competition is therefore protocol-dependent, and does not establish measurement replacement, statistical equivalence or a label-to-record exchange rate.

replacements.before: Second, the transfer protocol matters. Quantitative supervision was stronger for direct zero-shot ranking on Q-HERO and OOD-17, whereas expert supervision still supplied a positive potency-related rank signal without observing concentrations. Direct R² was negative for the quantitative models and the apparent improvement after affine recalibration was fitted on the same target predictions; it is exploratory rather than evidence of generalisable calibration. OOD-17 estimates require caution because n = 17.
replacements.after: Direct transfer provides complementary evidence: the expert model receives binary training targets rather than concentrations, yet its scores rank measured potency on the evaluation collections. Quantitative MIC supervision gives stronger direct ranking on Q-HERO and OOD-17. Numerical MIC calibration and ranking are distinct tasks; the archived affine recalibration is in-sample and exploratory, and the 17-compound OOD estimates remain imprecise.

replacements.before: Third, archived representational analyses are consistent with substantial retention of the pretrained MolFormer geometry, but the SHAP and CKA provenance is incomplete. We therefore do not claim a quantified causal biological component. Future work should retain individual annotation votes, use molecule-grouped external splits, preregister a non-inferiority margin, and evaluate calibration on held-out target data. Priority claims about this supervision design also require an external literature review before submission.
replacements.after: The defensible causal claim concerns changing supervision within a fixed computational procedure. The new real-versus-shuffled control supports this claim in one defined panel; it does not identify a biological mechanism or prove that human judgement removes assay heterogeneity. Individual annotation votes, annotation cost, prospective performance and a pre-specified non-inferiority criterion are unavailable. The results motivate testing human labels as a compact supervision signal while specifying the task, source chemistry, training procedure and transfer regime in which they are competitive.

added_sections: 2.6 Controlled supervision interventions and quantitative-source comparisons

The partial-fine-tuning results demonstrate practical competition, but they do not isolate supervision content because the sources differ in molecule count and training objective. We therefore ran an additional frozen-MolFormer experiment with a 768→256→128 neural encoder and identical source molecules within each comparison panel. All target cations, including counterion variants, were excluded from every source. Conflicting expert labels were removed. The new evaluation cohorts comprise 104 non-conflicting in-domain salts, 405 non-conflicting Q-HERO salts after target-cation overlap removal, and the 17-compound OOD set. These stricter cohorts and the frozen-backbone architecture differ from the partial-fine-tuning experiment and are reported separately.

The pooled-MIC panel contains 681 common molecules with 4,938 underlying records; the exact S. aureus panel contains 529 common molecules with 855 records. Within each panel we compare real expert labels, continuous MIC, MIC binarised at a source-training threshold targeting the expert positive prevalence, permuted expert labels, permuted continuous MIC and an untrained encoder. MIC ties prevent exact prevalence matching. Five paired initialisation seeds, one shared scaffold-disjoint source split and 80 fixed training epochs are used. Target scaffold folds and downstream decoder settings are identical across arms. The source validation partition is diagnostic and does not select a checkpoint.

For the pooled panel, mean Q-HERO-405 CatBoost RMSE is 1.607 for expert labels, 1.497 for continuous MIC, 1.646 for binary MIC and 1.780 for shuffled expert labels (Table 3). The paired expert-minus-shuffled-expert difference is −0.175 log2 µM, with a 95% whole-scaffold bootstrap interval of [−0.258, −0.058]. This control shows that the real label assignment matters in this panel. Expert supervision is not measurably better than raw MolFormer: ΔRMSE = +0.005 [−0.092, +0.109]. Nor does it outperform continuous MIC: expert minus continuous MIC is +0.109 [+0.007, +0.210]. The expert-versus-binary-MIC interval includes zero (−0.039 [−0.139, +0.136]); it is not an equivalence result.

On the smaller S. aureus-matched panel, the expert-label benefit does not reproduce. Mean Q-HERO RMSE is 1.785 for real expert labels, 1.761 for shuffled expert labels and 1.617 for continuous MIC. Expert minus shuffled labels is +0.025 [−0.139, +0.311], and expert minus continuous MIC is +0.169 [−0.004, +0.454]. Restricting the panel changes the selected chemical collection as well as its size; this contrast cannot identify an organism-matching effect. The result sets a clear limit: transferable expert information and practical competition do not imply a consistent benefit from every expert-trained encoder.

Table 3. New matched-molecule supervision experiment on Q-HERO-405 with a CatBoost decoder, mean ± standard deviation over five source-training seeds. Pooled MIC and exact S. aureus MIC use separate common-molecule panels. Reported seed variation is not a confidence interval across independent chemical datasets. Paired molecule- and scaffold-bootstrap contrasts, all secondary targets, and the Ridge sensitivity analysis are supplied in Supporting Information Section S7.

The practical full-source comparison uses 712 expert-labelled molecules, 1,120 pooled-MIC molecules, 888 exact S. aureus-MIC molecules and 273 ILToxDB cytotoxicity molecules. Mean Q-HERO R² is 0.095, 0.246, 0.185 and 0.083, respectively (Figure 7d). These results extend the comparison to several numerical supervision definitions, including an independent cytotoxicity source, but show that expert supervision does not uniformly match the best quantitative arm in the frozen-head setting. Because source size, coverage, label definition and experimental context differ, the ranking is a practical observation rather than a causal effect of endpoint or provenance.

Figure 7. Protocol dependence of expert supervision. (a) Archived partial fine-tuning yields competitive downstream representation quality on Q-HERO (three seeds). (b,c) New matched-molecule frozen-backbone interventions on pooled and exact S. aureus MIC panels; bars show 95% paired whole-scaffold bootstrap intervals conditional on five trained seeds and fixed target folds. Negative ΔRMSE favours human labels. (d) New full-source comparison has unequal source sizes and cannot isolate endpoint or provenance. Panels use different cohorts and architectures and must not be interpreted as one interchangeable leaderboard.

The causal estimand is the change in external predictive loss when a supervision assignment/objective is replaced within this fixed training pipeline. Both predictions are observed for each held-out molecule under paired runs, so a paired loss contrast is sufficient; a causal forest fitted to duplicated prediction rows would add no identification. Real-versus-permuted expert labels preserve molecule identities, class counts, architecture and training budget while disrupting the structure–label relation. The five shuffled runs are diagnostic controls, not a calibrated multi-permutation hypothesis test. The experiment supplies bounded evidence about algorithmic supervision content; it does not show that experts identify membrane-disruption mechanisms or remove laboratory bias.

Quantitative-source interpretation also requires care. The local QMR same-compound/same-strain audit contains 38 replicate strata over only 23 compounds and five strains: median log2 range is zero, with 94.7% within one dilution. Within-group variation across S. aureus strains has median range 1 log2 unit over 279 strata. These selectively available replicates do not establish universal assay reproducibility, but they do prevent the pooled conflict rate from being interpreted as a pure inter-laboratory error rate. Likewise, the Q-HERO/QMR/ILToxDB transfer contrasts remain confounded by source selection, chemical composition, assay context and aggregation. Human labels as robust compression of heterogeneous evidence remain an explanation to test, rather than an established cause of their performance.
